claim: The inducible innate immune response to infection requires a concerted process of gene expression that is regulated at multiple levels.
source: The inducible innate immune response to infection requires a concerted process of gene expression that is regulated at multiple levels.
evidence: This is a general statement about immune response that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Most global analyses of the innate immune response have focused on transcription induced by defined immunostimulatory ligands, such as lipopolysaccharide.
source: Most global analyses of the innate immune response have focused on transcription induced by defined immunostimulatory ligands, such as lipopolysaccharide.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field that draws from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Pathogens interfere with virtually every step of gene expression.
source: However, the response to pathogens involves additional complexity, as pathogens interfere with virtually every step of gene expression.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work in the field.

claim: A pathogen-mediated blockade of host protein synthesis provokes the production of specific pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: We previously discovered that a pathogen-mediated blockade of host protein synthesis provokes the production of specific pro-inflammatory cytokines.
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous published work.

claim: mRNA superinduction is required for the inducible immune response to a bacterial pathogen.
source: Our results reveal that mRNA superinduction is required for the inducible immune response to a bacterial pathogen.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Changes in mRNA levels accounted for ~90% of observed alterations in protein levels in dendritic cells responding to LPS.
source: One recent study analyzed the response of dendritic cells to lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and found that changes in mRNA levels accounted for ~90% of observed alterations in protein levels (Jovanovic et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific published study.

claim: Pathogens have evolved to disrupt or manipulate almost every cellular process involved in gene expression.
source: Indeed, pathogens have evolved to disrupt or manipulate almost every cellular process involved in gene expression (Finlay and McFadden, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Inhibition of host protein synthesis is a common strategy used by many viral and bacterial pathogens to disrupt host gene expression.
source: Inhibition of host protein synthesis is a common strategy used by many viral and bacterial pathogens to disrupt host gene expression (Mohr and Sonenberg, 2012; Lemaitre and Girardin, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: L. pneumophila uses its Dot/Icm type IV secretion system (T4SS) to translocate into host cells several effector proteins that block host protein synthesis.
source: For example, the intracellular bacterial pathogen L. pneumophila uses its Dot/Icm type IV secretion system (T4SS) to translocate into host cells several effector proteins that block host protein synthesis, including at least four effectors that target the elongation factor eEF1A (Lemaitre and Girardin, 2013; Barry et al., 2013; Belyi et al., 2008; Fontana et al., 2011; Shen et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Pseudomonas aeruginosa blocks host translation elongation by secretion of exotoxin A.
source: Similarly, the bacterial pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa blocks host translation elongation by secretion of exotoxin A (Lemaitre and Girardin, 2013; Dunbar et al., 2012; Iglewski et al., 1977).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Host cells respond to protein synthesis inhibition by initiating a specific host response characterized by production of specific pro-inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-23 (Il23a), granulocyte macrophage colony-stimulating factor (Csf2) and interleukin-1α (Il1a).
source: Interestingly, we previously discovered that host cells respond to protein synthesis inhibition — whether by Legionella, exotoxin A, or by pharmacological agents that block translation initiation or elongation — by initiating a specific host response characterized by production of specific pro-inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-23 (Il23a), granulocyte macrophage colony-stimulating factor (Csf2) and interleukin-1α (Il1a) (Barry et al., 2013; Fontana et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement refers to the authors' previous published work.

claim: One model posits that the block in protein synthesis leads to superinduction of cytokine mRNAs that is sufficient to overcome the partial block in host protein synthesis.
source: One model posits that the block in protein synthesis leads to superinduction of cytokine mRNAs that is sufficient to overcome the partial block in host protein synthesis (Barry et al., 2013; Fontana et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement describes a model proposed in prior work by the authors.

claim: It has been proposed that host cells may circumvent the global block in protein synthesis by selective translation of specific cytokine transcripts.
source: Alternatively, it has been proposed that host cells may circumvent the global block in protein synthesis by selective translation of specific cytokine transcripts (Dunbar et al., 2012; Asrat et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement describes an alternative model proposed in prior work.

claim: ~90% of macrophages were infected with at least one bacterium under the infection conditions used.
source: Control experiments demonstrated that ~90% of macrophages were infected with at least one bacterium under our infection conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Ribosome footprints were found to map preferentially to the exonic regions of infection-induced genes.
source: As a confirmation of the quality of the ribosome profiling libraries, ribosome footprints were found to map preferentially to the exonic regions of infection-induced genes (Figure 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Ribosome footprints showed a strong bias toward 27–28 nucleotide fragment lengths.
source: ribosome footprints were found to map preferentially to the exonic regions of infection-induced genes (Figure 1), and showed a strong bias toward 27–28 nucleotide fragment lengths (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), consistent with the known size of ribosome-protected footprints.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and is consistent with known properties of ribosome footprints.

claim: Induction of ribosome footprints on Gem, Csf2, and Il23a required the seven-bacterial effectors associated with the block in host protein synthesis.
source: In accord with previous studies, induction of ribosome footprints on Gem, Csf2, and Il23a required the seven-bacterial effectors associated with the block in host protein synthesis, while induction of ribosome footprints corresponding to Il1a and Il1b required the bacterial T4SS (Figure 1A–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A–F.

claim: Induction of ribosome footprints corresponding to Il1a and Il1b required the bacterial T4SS.
source: In accord with previous studies, induction of ribosome footprints on Gem, Csf2, and Il23a required the seven-bacterial effectors associated with the block in host protein synthesis, while induction of ribosome footprints corresponding to Il1a and Il1b required the bacterial T4SS (Figure 1A–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A–F.

claim: The majority of T4SS-dependent increases in ribosome footprints could be explained at the level of mRNA induction.
source: We found that the majority of T4SS-dependent increases in ribosome footprints could be explained at the level of mRNA induction, as there was nearly a perfect linear correlation between the extent of mRNA induction and ribosome footprints for all T4SS-induced genes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A showing a linear correlation.

claim: There was nearly a perfect linear correlation between the extent of mRNA induction and ribosome footprints for all T4SS-induced genes.
source: We found that the majority of T4SS-dependent increases in ribosome footprints could be explained at the level of mRNA induction, as there was nearly a perfect linear correlation between the extent of mRNA induction and ribosome footprints for all T4SS-induced genes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A robust correlation was observed between the extent of mRNA induction and the extent of protein induction in cell lysates.
source: We observed a robust correlation between the extent of mRNA induction and the extent of protein induction, particularly in lysates (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The correlation between mRNA levels and protein levels applies for the most highly induced proteins/mRNAs (e.g. IL-10 (Il10) and GM-CSF (Csf2)) but also for more modestly induced cytokines (Il1a, Il1b, Cxcl10).
source: The correlation seems to apply for the most highly induced proteins/mRNAs (e.g. IL-10 (Il10) and GM-CSF (Csf2)) but also for more modestly induced cytokines (Il1a, Il1b, Cxcl10).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: The less robust correlation between mRNA levels and protein levels in the cell supernatant may reflect differing rates of secretion, accumulation in the supernatant over time, re-binding to cell surface receptors, and stability in the supernatant.
source: The less robust correlation between mRNA levels and protein levels in the cell supernatant (Figure 2C) may reflect differing rates of secretion, accumulation in the supernatant over time, re-binding to cell surface receptors, and stability in the supernatant.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data pattern.

claim: The inducible immune response to L. pneumophila is controlled primarily at the level of mRNA superinduction.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the inducible immune response to L. pneumophila is controlled primarily at the level of mRNA superinduction (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The ∆7 strain that lacks seven bacterial effectors is still able to partially suppress host protein synthesis by a mechanism that remains to be fully characterized.
source: Interestingly, the ∆7 strain that lacks these effectors is still able to partially suppress host protein synthesis by a mechanism that remains to be fully characterized (Barry et al., 2013; Fontana et al., 2011; Ivanov and Roy, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: It has been proposed that T4SS-competent L. pneumophila damages host cell membranes, resulting in ubiquitylation-dependent downregulation of mTOR activity and a block in cap-dependent translation.
source: It has been proposed that T4SS-competent L. pneumophila damages host cell membranes, resulting in ubiquitylation-dependent downregulation of mTOR activity and a block in cap-dependent translation (Ivanov and Roy, 2013).
evidence: This statement describes a model proposed in prior work.

claim: The ∆7 strain still provokes IL-1α production, although its ability to stimulate Il23a and Csf2 expression is diminished.
source: Consistent with its ability to partially suppress protein synthesis, the ∆7 strain still provokes IL-1α production, although its ability to stimulate Il23a and Csf2 expression is diminished (Barry et al., 2013; Fontana et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Induction of Gem, Il23a, and Csf2 is highly dependent on the seven bacterial effectors.
source: As expected, induction of Gem, Il23a, and Csf2 is highly dependent on the seven bacterial effectors, but again, similar to the total T4SS-dependent gene induction (Figure 2), the seven effector-dependent induction of ribosome footprints on these genes could be explained at the level of mRNA induction (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The seven effector-dependent induction of ribosome footprints on Gem, Il23a, and Csf2 could be explained at the level of mRNA induction.
source: As expected, induction of Gem, Il23a, and Csf2 is highly dependent on the seven bacterial effectors, but again, similar to the total T4SS-dependent gene induction (Figure 2), the seven effector-dependent induction of ribosome footprints on these genes could be explained at the level of mRNA induction (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: All changes in ribosome footprint reads for Dusp1, Dusp2, Cxcl1, Cxcl2, Tnf, Il1a, Il1b, and Il6 could be explained by changes in mRNA levels.
source: While the seven effector-dependent induction of the genes Dusp1, Dusp2, Cxcl1, Cxcl2, Tnf, Il1a, Il1b, and Il6 was low, all changes in ribosome footprint reads could again be explained by changes in mRNA levels (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: T4SS-dependent and seven bacterial effector-dependent induction of inflammatory cytokines occurs by the induction of mRNA transcripts rather than through a mechanism of selective ribosome loading of mRNAs.
source: These data suggest that T4SS-dependent and seven bacterial effector-dependent induction of inflammatory cytokines occurs by the induction of mRNA transcripts rather than through a mechanism of selective ribosome loading of mRNAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: It was previously proposed that specific transcripts, such as Il1a and Il1b, can be preferentially translated via a mechanism that requires signaling through the adaptor protein MyD88.
source: It was previously proposed that specific transcripts, such as Il1a and Il1b, can be preferentially translated via a mechanism that requires signaling through the adaptor protein MyD88 (Asrat et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement describes a model proposed in prior work.

claim: For all MyD88-induced genes, including Il1a and Il1b, a linear correlation was observed between the induction of ribosome footprints and RNAseq reads.
source: For all MyD88-induced genes, including Il1a and Il1b, we observed a linear correlation between the induction of ribosome footprints and RNAseq reads (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: MyD88-dependent induction of Il1a and Il1b ribosome footprints is controlled primarily at the level of mRNA induction, rather than at the level of selective ribosome loading of the mRNA.
source: This implies that MyD88-dependent induction of Il1a and Il1b ribosome footprints is controlled primarily at the level of mRNA induction, rather than at the level of selective ribosome loading of the mRNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: The ability of host cells to overcome a pathogen-induced block in protein synthesis, and produce inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1α and IL-1β, requires a T4SS- and MyD88-dependent increase in mRNA levels rather than preferential loading of these cytokine mRNAs with ribosomes.
source: Taken together, our results argue that the ability of host cells to overcome a pathogen-induced block in protein synthesis, and produce inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1α and IL-1β, requires a T4SS- and MyD88-dependent increase in mRNA levels rather than preferential loading of these cytokine mRNAs with ribosomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: There is a wide range of ribosome occupancies across different transcripts.
source: This analysis revealed a wide range of ribosome occupancies across different transcripts (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A–D.

claim: Many of the mRNAs with the highest ribosome occupancy encoded abundant 'housekeeping' proteins, including Acta1 and histone mRNAs (e.g. Hist1h2ba, H2afj, and Hist3h2ba).
source: As might be anticipated, many of the mRNAs with the highest ribosome occupancy encoded abundant 'housekeeping' proteins, including Acta1 and histone mRNAs (e.g. Hist1h2ba, H2afj, and Hist3h2ba) (Figure 4A; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Table 1.

claim: Most mRNAs that exhibit increased ribosome occupancy in uninfected BMMs also exhibit increased ribosome occupancy in ΔflaA, ΔdotAΔflaA, or Δ7ΔflaA L. pneumophila-infected BMMs.
source: Importantly, most mRNAs that exhibit increased ribosome occupancy in uninfected BMMs also exhibit increased ribosome occupancy in ΔflaA, ΔdotAΔflaA, or Δ7ΔflaA L. pneumophila-infected BMMs (Figure 4B–D; Table 1), implying that the increased ribosome occupancy of these mRNAs is constitutive and not induced in response to infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B–D and Table 1.

claim: The increased ribosome occupancy of certain mRNAs is constitutive and not induced in response to infection.
source: Importantly, most mRNAs that exhibit increased ribosome occupancy in uninfected BMMs also exhibit increased ribosome occupancy in ΔflaA, ΔdotAΔflaA, or Δ7ΔflaA L. pneumophila-infected BMMs (Figure 4B–D; Table 1), implying that the increased ribosome occupancy of these mRNAs is constitutive and not induced in response to infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 4B–D and Table 1.

claim: Lyz1, S100a11, and Cxcl3 exhibited elevated ribosome occupancy in all infection conditions.
source: A few mRNAs of immunological interest, namely Lyz1, S100a11, and Cxcl3 exhibited elevated ribosome occupancy in all infection conditions (Figure 4B–D; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B–D and Table 1.

claim: Ftl1 mRNA exhibited very low ribosome occupancy.
source: In contrast, Ftl1 mRNA exhibited very low ribosome occupancy (Figure 4A), consistent with a previous report showing that Ftl1 translation can be strongly repressed (Cairo et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and is consistent with prior work.

claim: Ftl1 translation can be strongly repressed.
source: In contrast, Ftl1 mRNA exhibited very low ribosome occupancy (Figure 4A), consistent with a previous report showing that Ftl1 translation can be strongly repressed (Cairo et al., 1989).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Atf4 is a gene known to be regulated at the level of translation.
source: Atf4 is another gene known to be regulated at the level of translation (Pavitt and Ron, 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In ΔflaA and ΔdotAΔflaA L. pneumophila-infected BMMs, Atf4 exhibited low ribosome occupancy.
source: and in ΔflaA and ΔdotAΔflaA L. pneumophila-infected BMMs, Atf4 exhibited low ribosome occupancy (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B–C.

claim: Several mRNAs exhibit constitutive increased or decreased ribosome occupancy.
source: Taken together, our results reveal that several mRNAs exhibit constitutive increased or decreased ribosome occupancy, as expected.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: Ribosome occupancy of mRNAs was not markedly affected by L. pneumophila infection.
source: Despite this, ribosome occupancy of mRNAs was not markedly affected by L. pneumophila infection (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 4A–D.

claim: All metagene plots demonstrated a characteristic three-nucleotide periodicity.
source: As expected from the known stepwise codon-by-codon movement of the ribosome, all metagene plots demonstrated a characteristic three-nucleotide periodicity (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5 and is consistent with known properties of ribosome movement.

claim: Metagene ribosome profiles of uninfected, ΔflaA, ΔdotAΔflaA, or Δ7ΔflaA infected BMMs appeared grossly similar to each other.
source: Interestingly, metagene ribosome profiles of uninfected (Figure 5A–B), ΔflaA (Figure 5C–D), ΔdotAΔflaA (Figure 5E–F), or Δ7ΔflaA (Figure 5G–H) infected BMMs appeared grossly similar to each other, even though global translation is blocked only in the ΔflaA and Δ7ΔflaA L. pneumophila-infected conditions (Barry et al., 2013; Fontana et al., 2011; Asrat et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5 and citations to prior work.

claim: Global translation is blocked only in the ΔflaA and Δ7ΔflaA L. pneumophila-infected conditions.
source: Interestingly, metagene ribosome profiles of uninfected (Figure 5A–B), ΔflaA (Figure 5C–D), ΔdotAΔflaA (Figure 5E–F), or Δ7ΔflaA (Figure 5G–H) infected BMMs appeared grossly similar to each other, even though global translation is blocked only in the ΔflaA and Δ7ΔflaA L. pneumophila-infected conditions (Barry et al., 2013; Fontana et al., 2011; Asrat et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ribosome metagene profiles do not distinguish whether ribosome footprints arise from stalled or translating ribosomes, unless the stall occurs at a characteristic distance from the start or stop codon.
source: This result can be explained by the fact that ribosome metagene profiles do not distinguish whether ribosome footprints arise from stalled or translating ribosomes, unless the stall occurs at a characteristic distance from the start or stop codon.
evidence: This is an explanation based on knowledge of the ribosome profiling technique.

claim: There was a slight increase in the number of ribosomes found at the start site of the transcript in Δ7ΔflaA L. pneumophila-infected BMMs as compared to other conditions.
source: In fact, we did notice a slight increase in the number of ribosomes found at the start site of the transcript in Δ7ΔflaA L. pneumophila-infected BMMs as compared to other conditions (Figure 5I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The slight increase in ribosomes at the start site in Δ7ΔflaA L. pneumophila-infected BMMs may reflect a selective block in translation initiation by this strain.
source: This may reflect a selective block in translation initiation by this strain (see below).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: In all conditions, ribosomes accumulated at the stop codon.
source: In addition, we noted that in all conditions, ribosomes accumulated at the stop codon, suggesting that, in BMMs, translation termination may be a limiting step in translation (Figure 5J).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: In BMMs, translation termination may be a limiting step in translation.
source: In addition, we noted that in all conditions, ribosomes accumulated at the stop codon, suggesting that, in BMMs, translation termination may be a limiting step in translation (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Harringtonine inhibits the first rounds of peptide bond formation following ribosome subunit joining and results in accumulation of ribosomes at the translational start site and run-off of elongating (but not stalled) ribosomes that have already cleared the start codon.
source: Harringtonine inhibits the first rounds of peptide bond formation following ribosome subunit joining and results in accumulation of ribosomes at the translational start site and run-off of elongating (but not stalled) ribosomes that have already cleared the start codon (Ingolia et al., 2012, 2011; Huang and Harringtonine, 1975; Tscherne and Pestka, 1975; Fresno et al., 1977).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cells experiencing a block in translation elongation will exhibit less ribosome run-off after harringtonine treatment, and an increased number of reads at the 5ʹ end of mRNAs after drug treatment.
source: Importantly, cells experiencing a block in translation elongation will exhibit less ribosome run-off after harringtonine treatment, and an increased number of reads at the 5ʹ end of mRNAs after drug treatment (Ingolia et al., 2011), compared to cells in which elongation is not blocked.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Uninfected and ΔdotAΔflaA-infected BMMs show an increase in ribosome footprints at the translation start site and a preferential loss of ribosome footprints from the 5ʹ and 3ʹ end of mRNAs, consistent with the expected effects of harringtonine and demonstrating clear ribosome run-off.
source: As expected, uninfected and ΔdotAΔflaA-infected BMMs show an increase in ribosome footprints at the translation start site and a preferential loss of ribosome footprints from the 5ʹ and 3ʹ end of mRNAs, consistent with the expected effects of harringtonine and demonstrating clear ribosome run-off (Figure 6A–B,E–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A–B,E–F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: ΔflaA L. pneumophila-infected BMMs treated with harringtonine exhibited little ribosome run-off.
source: By contrast, ΔflaA L. pneumophila-infected BMMs treated with harringtonine exhibited little ribosome run-off (Figure 6C–D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B), consistent with the expectation that ΔflaA L. pneumophila blocks host translation elongation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C–D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: ΔflaA L. pneumophila blocks host translation elongation.
source: By contrast, ΔflaA L. pneumophila-infected BMMs treated with harringtonine exhibited little ribosome run-off (Figure 6C–D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B), consistent with the expectation that ΔflaA L. pneumophila blocks host translation elongation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 6C–D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Clear evidence of run-off of elongating ribosomes from the 5ʹ and 3ʹ end of mRNAs was observed following harringtonine treatment in Δ7ΔflaA L. pneumophila-infected BMMs.
source: The Δ7ΔflaA L. pneumophila strain, lacking all known bacterial effectors that block host protein synthesis, nevertheless, shuts down host translation (Barry et al., 2013), yet we observed clear evidence of run-off of elongating ribosomes from the 5ʹ and 3ʹ end of mRNAs following harringtonine treatment (Figure 6G–H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6G–H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: The residual block in host protein synthesis induced by Δ7ΔflaA L. pneumophila is at the level of translation initiation.
source: These data suggest that the residual block in host protein synthesis induced by Δ7ΔflaA L. pneumophila is at the level of translation initiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 6G–H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: It is unlikely that uninfected bystander cells are responsible for the ribosome run-off seen in Δ7ΔflaA L. pneumophila-infected BMMs because the conditions used in these experiments led to most (~90%) cells being infected with L. pneumophila.
source: However, it is unlikely that these uninfected cells are responsible for the ribosome run-off seen in Δ7ΔflaA L. pneumophila-infected BMMs because the conditions used in these experiments led to most (~90%) cells being infected with L. pneumophila (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the infectivity data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: If infection conditions resulted in large numbers of uninfected cells, then a similar run-off should have been observed in the ∆flaA-infected sample, which it was not.
source: Furthermore, if our infection conditions resulted in large numbers of uninfected cells, then a similar run-off should have been observed in the ∆flaA-infected sample, which it was not.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the data.

claim: The seven effectors are required to block translation elongation.
source: Thus, these results suggest that the seven effectors are required to block translation elongation, and that the residual translation inhibition induced by Δ7ΔflaA L. pneumophila is at the level of translation initiation (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Uninfected, ΔdotAΔflaA, and Δ7ΔflaA-infected BMMs show a clear global signature of ribosome run-off.
source: Consistent with our previous analysis, we find that uninfected, ΔdotAΔflaA, and Δ7ΔflaA-infected BMMs show a clear global signature of ribosome run-off, again suggesting that the block in host protein synthesis induced by Δ7ΔflaA L. pneumophila infection is occurring at the level of translation initiation (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A–D.

claim: In ΔflaA-infected BMMs there is no evidence of ribosome run-off, consistent with ΔflaA L. pneumophila inducing a block in host translation elongation.
source: Importantly, in ΔflaA-infected BMMs there is no evidence of ribosome run-off, consistent with ΔflaA L. pneumophila inducing a block in host translation elongation (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In all conditions tested, cytokine-related genes fell well within the average of ribosome retention across all transcripts, and if anything, were found to have reduced ribosome run-off compared to a typical gene.
source: Interestingly, in all conditions tested, cytokine-related genes fell well within the average of ribosome retention across all transcripts, and if anything, were found to have reduced ribosome run-off compared to a typical gene (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A–D.

claim: At this time point, cytokine transcripts are not preferentially translated in response to pathogenic infection, but instead are controlled at the level of mRNA induction.
source: These results imply that at this time point, cytokine transcripts are not preferentially translated in response to pathogenic infection, but instead are controlled at the level of mRNA induction (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 7A–D.

claim: A recent study showed that in response to innate immune stimulation with purified LPS, dendritic cells almost entirely control the induction of genes at the level of transcription.
source: A recent study showed that in response to innate immune stimulation with purified LPS, dendritic cells almost entirely control the induction of genes at the level of transcription (Jovanovic et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Pathogen-induced blockade of host protein synthesis has been shown in a number of infection models to be sensed by the host and induce an inflammatory response.
source: Pathogen-induced blockade of host protein synthesis has been shown in a number of infection models to be sensed by the host and induce an inflammatory response (Barry et al., 2013; Fontana et al., 2011; Dunbar et al., 2012; McEwan et al., 2012; Chakrabarti et al., 2012; Fontana et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: IL-1α was identified as a key inflammatory cytokine induced preferentially in response to translation inhibition imposed by L. pneumophila.
source: We previously identified IL-1α as a key inflammatory cytokine induced preferentially in response to translation inhibition imposed by L. pneumophila (Barry et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement refers to the authors' previous published work.

claim: Translation inhibition results in a failure to synthesize negative feedback inhibitors of transcription, for example, IκB or A20.
source: We previously provided evidence for a model in which translation inhibition results in a failure to synthesize negative feedback inhibitors of transcription, for example, IκB or A20 (Fontana et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement refers to the authors' previous published work.

claim: Massive and sustained production of cytokine transcripts, termed mRNA superinduction, is sufficient to overcome the partial (~95%) block in translation and allow for production of cytokine proteins.
source: We proposed this results in a massive and sustained production of cytokine transcripts, termed mRNA superinduction, that is sufficient to overcome the partial (~95%) block in translation and allow for production of cytokine proteins (Barry et al., 2013; Fontana et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement refers to the authors' previous published work.

claim: Another report provided data suggesting that IL-1 production is mediated by MyD88-enhanced protein synthesis.
source: Another report provided data suggesting that IL-1 production is mediated by MyD88-enhanced protein synthesis, although alternative explanations were also entertained (Asrat et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement describes findings from prior work.

claim: A third study proposed that virulent L. pneumophila regulates cap-dependent translation initiation, via manipulation of the mTOR signaling pathway, to regulate the protein levels of highly abundant transcripts in infected macrophages.
source: A third study proposed that virulent L. pneumophila regulates cap-dependent translation initiation, via manipulation of the mTOR signaling pathway, to regulate the protein levels of highly abundant transcripts in infected macrophages (Ivanov and Roy, 2013).
evidence: This statement describes a model proposed in prior work.

claim: The induction of ribosome footprints by L. pneumophila could be explained by an underlying induction of mRNAs.
source: In our present study, we found that the induction of ribosome footprints by L. pneumophila could be explained by an underlying induction of mRNAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There was no evidence found for selective ribosome loading of abundant cytokine mRNAs.
source: We did not find evidence for selective ribosome loading of abundant cytokine mRNAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ribosome run-off experiments confirmed that cytokine mRNAs are not selectively translated during infection.
source: In addition, ribosome run-off experiments confirmed that cytokine mRNAs are not selectively translated during infection (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 7.

source: Thus, in contrast to a previous study that used virus-based translation reporter experiments in L. pneumophila-infected RAW macrophages (Ivanov and Roy, 2013), we were clearly able to dissociate the L. pneumophila-induced block in host protein synthesis into two components: (1) an elongation block that required the seven translocated effectors, and (2) an initiation block that did not require the seven effectors.
